extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, prosecutors, and in-house counsel evaluating U.S. §101 patent-eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-law standards for determining patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), with examples from district and Federal Circuit decisions across software, business-method, and biotech patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are treated as 'directed to' an abstract idea when their character is essentially a fundamental practice, mental process, or longstanding commercial practice (e.g., collecting/organizing/analyzing data; receiving/transmitting information; business transactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page repeatedly holds claims directed to abstract ideas such as 'selecting a program, verifying whether the program is licensed, and acting on the program according to the verification'; 'collecting, organizing, and analyzing medical claims data to calculate physician efficiency scores'; 'receipt, processing, and display of data'; 'selling, gifting, and using an electronic gift certificate'; 'time stamping'; 'coordinating and monitoring baggage delivery.' These holdings show that data-collection/analysis, basic information transfer, business/financial practices, and analogous human mental activities are paradigmatically 'abstract ideas.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of inventive concept (Alice step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is directed to an abstract idea, it is ineligible unless the claim recites an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated holdings state claims lacked an inventive concept because they merely implemented the abstract idea on generic technology or used routine steps (e.g., 'with no inventive concept'; 'claims lacked an inventive concept because the recited amplification and detection steps were "well-understood, routine and conventional."').

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims covering laws of nature/natural phenomena are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to natural laws or natural phenomena (e.g., existence of cffDNA in maternal blood, correlations in DNA sequences, primers indistinguishable from nucleotide sequences) are treated as ineligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biotech examples: claims directed to the natural phenomenon of cffDNA, BRCA sequence comparisons, linkage disequilibrium principles, and primers have been held ineligible. Courts emphasize that discovery of a natural correlation alone does not render a claim patentable absent an inventive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine, conventional, well-understood techniques do not supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps that employ known, routine, or well-understood techniques (even if combined with a new discovery) do not contribute an inventive concept for eligibility purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: amplification and detection steps characterized as routine; using "well-known ASR technology" for speech recognition; recited compression/encryption/storage steps that give functional results without technical detail. Courts frequently find no inventive concept where the claim merely instructs to apply conventional techniques to an abstract idea or natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes/entirely in-the-mind steps are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim steps that can be performed entirely in the human mind or are essentially mental processes are treated as abstract and ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holdings include claims characterized as 'mental process' steps (e.g., recognizing words and storing results in report fields; interpreting a written social-media statement) and other examples such as calculating scores, comparing sequences, or making determinations that are essentially mental acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation does not make an idea patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying an abstract idea to the Internet or a generic computer (e.g., 'applying these concepts to internet traffic') is insufficient to confer eligibility unless the claim recites a specific technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: claims using a 'persistent identifier' for targeted marketing, or 'applying these concepts to internet traffic' were held abstract; 'applying these concepts to internet traffic does not take the patent outside of the realm of an abstract idea.' Mere computer implementation or use of networked devices is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that improve computer technology or solve a technical problem may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are tied to a particular technological improvement or solve a problem rooted in computer technology can be found not directed to an abstract idea and thus may be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where courts denied dismissal: a computer application upgrade that solved a problem in digital distribution by generating unique installation patches for release channels; transcription error recognition claims that 'recite[d] specific methods for navigating and editing dictation transcripts' and thus 'improve[d] the functionality of speech recognition devices.' Such claims include specific technical means, not merely abstract ideas implemented on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific limiting rules tied to a technical field can weigh toward eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite detailed, field-specific processing rules or feature extraction methods tied to digital image processing (or other technical domains) may be found to recite more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: photographic subject determination claims requiring 'extraction of both structural and semantic saliency features, and 'integrating' those features' were described as 'tied to digital image processing' and alleged to be 'unconventional' in the field—supporting a conclusion they might claim a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption of a fundamental practice/fundamental economic practice indicates ineligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effectively preempt an entire fundamental practice or economic/business method (e.g., 'conducting business electronically', 'balancing rights of content owners and consumers') are treated as abstract and ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases found ineligibility where claims simply computerized traditional paper-based ordering/ordering-management, general electronic financial recordkeeping, or other core commercial practices without an inventive concept or technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automating human activities using generic computing often remains abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely automate tasks previously performed by humans (e.g., replacing human labor with computer processing) are often characterized as directed to an abstract idea absent a specific technical innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims described as 'using a computer, instead of human labor, to combine two types of data to form machine code' were held directed to an abstract idea with no inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must supply technical detail showing how results are achieved to support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that state functional results without technical detail describing how to achieve those results are vulnerable to §101 invalidity for lacking an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court holdings reference claims that 'obtain[ed] functional results' (e.g., 'determining a parameter, selecting a compression algorithm, applying that algorithm, and storing the resulting data') but provided 'no technical detail describing how to achieve those results' and were thus ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient factual development on unconventionality can preclude immediate dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the complaint or specification alleges that a claimed process was unconventional in its field, courts may deny motions to dismiss to allow factual development on whether the claims contain an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: courts denied dismissal where plaintiffs alleged a novel approach or that the claimed module operated in an unconventional way (e.g., home social newsfeed generation, photographic feature integration), noting that 'factual development regarding just how unconventional or innovative this application was at the time might impact the Section 101 inquiry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and expert evidence can affect the §101 analysis (but absence may not block early resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: While claim construction or expert testimony can be important, courts have held that a §101 decision can be appropriate early if the patent and pleadings show the claim is plainly directed to an abstract idea and lacks an inventive concept; conversely, lack of proposed constructions or expert support can permit dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Cleveland Clinic Foundation decision noted the appellant provided no proposed constructions or expert testimony that would change the eligibility analysis, supporting summary dismissal. Conversely, other decisions preserved claims where technical specificity or allegations might preclude early resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical or 'hardware' steps do not automatically save claims if they are conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting physical steps or components (e.g., amplifying, sensing, transmitting) does not avoid ineligibility where those physical steps are routine and conventional or add no inventive technical detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biotech and software examples: amplification and analysis steps in DNA-related claims were deemed routine; claims reciting sending/receiving commands to operate EV charging stations or downloading/storing encrypted data were held abstract when the physical operations contributed no inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims narrowly describing particular technical implementations may survive §101 at pleading stage
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims recite concrete technical limitations describing how to achieve improved functionality, courts may decline to dismiss on eligibility grounds pending factual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances where courts denied motions: claims that contained 'specific limiting rules' or described a 'specific method of producing guidance information for capturing an image' that was 'not necessarily conventional or generic'—these claims proceeded for further development rather than being dismissed as abstract.
